text:
Your direct traffic went up and you put it down to word of mouth.

Maybe. Or an AI recommended you to someone, they typed your name straight into the browser, and your analytics had nowhere to file it.

Those two things look identical in a report. They are not the same business.

One of them can stop next month and never tell you why.

Thirty-second job.

Open your analytics. Go to referrers. Search for chatgpt.com.

Most owners have never once looked. Whatever is sitting there, you have been running the business without it.

Your direct traffic is up. Nice. Most owners file that under word of mouth and move on.

Here's the other explanation.

Someone asked an AI for a recommendation. It named you. They didn't click anything, they just typed your name into the browser, because that's what people do when they've already been told who to call.

No referrer. No campaign. Nothing for your analytics to attach it to. So it lands in direct, next to the people who genuinely remembered you.

Word of mouth builds slowly and rarely collapses. A machine's recommendation can change the week a model updates, and you would watch the number fall without ever knowing what moved.

Same line on the graph. Completely different thing to be exposed to.

If you run marketing for other people, this one's going to sting.

You cannot invoice a flat line.

When an AI starts recommending your client, the leads arrive and your dashboard shows nothing. No channel, no campaign, no attribution. The client sees a quiet report and starts wondering what they're paying for, while the thing actually working sits in a column called direct.

You're not just losing credit for it. You're losing the argument about budget, because budget follows whatever has numbers next to it.

Your direct traffic isn't word of mouth.

Someone asked an AI who to use. It said you. They typed your name in. No referrer, so your analytics filed it under direct.

Go look at your referrers for chatgpt.com. Most people never have.
